theme: O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 7. David prays when he has been falsely accused. Notice how he asks God to judge him, and how he trusts the Judge of all the earth.
settingTheScene: The title reads, “A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjaminite.” We do not know who Cush was, but the setting is likely during the years when Saul, a Benjaminite, was pursuing David on false charges. The psalm is a cry for vindication from a man who has been slandered. It is placed here, right after the reading about Saul’s pursuit.
observation: “O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge; save me from all my pursuers and deliver me” (v. 1).
“O LORD my God, if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands… then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it” (vv. 3-5).
“Arise, O LORD, in your anger… awake for me; you have appointed a judgment” (v. 6).
“God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day” (v. 11).
“Behold, the wicked man conceives evil and is pregnant with mischief and gives birth to lies” (v. 14).
“He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made” (v. 15).
“His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends” (v. 16).
“I will give to the LORD the thanks due to his righteousness, and sing praise to the name of the LORD, the Most High” (v. 17).
interpretation:
David’s prayer here is bold. He asks God to examine him, and says that if he has done what his enemies say, then they may overtake him. This is not pride. It is a clear conscience before God on this particular charge. He is not claiming to be sinless, but he is saying that on this issue, he is innocent.

His great appeal is to God as judge. “God is a righteous judge.” When we are slandered, we are often tempted to take revenge or to defend ourselves at all costs. David takes the better way. He brings the case to the highest court and asks the Judge to rule. It is an act of trust, and it frees him from the need to retaliate. We will see this in his own behavior when he spares Saul’s life in the next chapters.

The image in verses 14 to 16 is memorable. The wicked person conceives, is pregnant with evil, and gives birth to lies. Evil has a life cycle. The person digs a pit for others, and falls into it himself. The universe has a moral structure, and sin often brings its own consequences. It is a warning to the wicked and a comfort to the wronged.

The psalm begins with refuge and ends with praise. The pattern is typical: David brings his case, rests it with God, and moves to thanksgiving before he has seen the verdict. The title of “Most High” for God reminds him that no earthly power can stand against the one who rules over everything.

The psalm is not an invitation to vindictiveness. It places justice in God’s hands. Paul would later say, “Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19).
connection: Jesus was falsely accused and “entrusted himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). He is the Righteous One, and he will return to judge the living and the dead (Acts 17:31). On the cross he committed his spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46). The wicked fall into their own pits, but the cross shows that God can turn even the pit into salvation (Acts 2:23-24).
application:
If you have been falsely accused or treated unjustly, bring the case to God rather than defending yourself in anger.

Search your own heart honestly, as David did. Is there anything you need to confess?

Give thanks that God is a righteous judge.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to search your heart and show you where you have sinned.
Leave in his hands a wrong done to you.
Thank Jesus for trusting the Father with his cause.
